source: Round 5 state trade licensing and code adoption (electrical, plumbing, HVAC) for NE-WY states, from official state board, statute, rule and code-adoption pages, checked October 2026

facts.source: Nebraska State Electrical Division, 2023 Code Adoption, https://electrical.nebraska.gov/2023-code-adoption
facts.fact: Nebraska's State Electrical Division adopted the 2023 National Electrical Code (NFPA 70) effective August 1, 2024. On that date, PSI electrical license exams and the in-office specialty exams also switched to the 2023 code.
facts.note: The division's State Act update notice (https://electrical.nebraska.gov/node/187) says PSI bulletins would allow either the 2020 or the 2023 NFPA 70 as a reference during the change.

facts.source: Nebraska State Electrical Division, Journeyman Electrician, https://electrical.nebraska.gov/node/44
facts.fact: A Nebraska journeyman electrician license requires at least four years (8,000 hours) of verifiable electrical experience acceptable to the State Electrical Board. A two-year post-high-school electrical course can count as one year of experience. An applicant with less than 4,000 hours of verifiable experience in Nebraska gets a restricted license, which cannot be used for reciprocity with other states.

facts.source: Nebraska State Electrical Division, Residential Journeyman Wireman, https://electrical.nebraska.gov/node/47
facts.fact: A Nebraska residential journeyman electrician (residential wireman) needs at least three years of electrical experience acceptable to the board. The license is valid only for residential work: one- and two-family homes and multi-family dwellings no more than three stories tall. Clubhouses at multi-family complexes must be wired by full (Type JA) journeymen.

facts.source: Nebraska State Electrical Division, Electrical Contractor, https://electrical.nebraska.gov/electrical-contractor
facts.fact: To qualify for a Nebraska electrical contractor license, an applicant needs at least one year of experience, acceptable to the board, as a licensed journeyman electrician. A graduate of a four-year electrical engineering program also needs at least one year as a licensed journeyman.

facts.source: Neb. Rev. Stat. 71-6403 and 71-6406, https://nebraskalegislature.gov/laws/statutes.php?statute=71-6403
facts.fact: Nebraska's state building code (Neb. Rev. Stat. 71-6403) adopts the 2018 IBC, the 2018 IRC (without section R313 and chapters 25-33), the 2018 IEBC and the 2018 Uniform Plumbing Code. Under 71-6406, the state code applies by default in any county, city or village that does not adopt its own code, and any local code must generally conform to the state code.
facts.note: Nebraska has no state plumbing license board; plumbing licenses come from cities such as Omaha and Lincoln (see existing fact STAT-244).

facts.source: Neb. Rev. Stat. 71-6403 and 71-6406, https://nebraskalegislature.gov/laws/statutes.php?statute=71-6406
facts.fact: Nebraska's state building code lists no mechanical or fuel gas code, and it leaves out the IRC's plumbing, mechanical and electrical chapters (25-33). Under 71-6406, cities, villages and counties may adopt mechanical and other standard codes themselves, so HVAC rules in Nebraska are set locally.
facts.note: Code contents verified in the statutes. The point that HVAC licensing is local only matches existing fact STAT-244, which is still unverified.

facts.source: NAC 624.200, Classification C-2: Electrical contracting (via Cornell LII), https://www.law.cornell.edu/regulations/nevada/NAC-624-200
facts.fact: The Nevada State Contractors Board licenses electrical contracting businesses under classification C-2. Its subclassifications are C-2a Electrical Wiring, C-2b Integrated Ceilings, C-2c Fire Detection, C-2d Low Voltage Systems, C-2e Lines to Transmit Electricity, C-2f Residential Wiring and C-2g Photovoltaics.
facts.note: Read from the Cornell LII copy of NAC 624.200. Nevada issues no statewide journeyman electrician license; worker cards, where required, come from local jurisdictions (not confirmed on an official page).

facts.source: NAC 624.190, Classification C-1: Plumbing and heating contracting (via Cornell LII), https://www.law.cornell.edu/regulations/nevada/NAC-624-190
facts.fact: Nevada licenses plumbing and heating contractors under NSCB classification C-1. Its subclassifications include C-1a Boilers, C-1b Fire Sprinklers, C-1c Insulation of Pipes and Ducts, C-1d Plumbing, C-1e Sheet Metal, C-1f Heating, Cooling and Circulating Air, C-1g Pipes and Vents for Gas, C-1h Water Heaters, C-1i Chilled-Water Piping, C-1j Breathing Air Systems for Firefighters and C-1k Industrial Piping.
facts.note: Read from the Cornell LII copy of NAC 624.190.

facts.source: NAC 624.380, Classification C-21: Refrigeration and air-conditioning (via Cornell LII), https://law.cornell.edu/regulations/nevada/NAC-624-380
facts.fact: Nevada's NSCB classification C-21 covers refrigeration and air-conditioning. Its subclassifications are C-21a Refrigeration, C-21b Air-Conditioning, C-21c Sheet Metal, C-21d Maintenance, C-21e Solar Air-Conditioning, C-21f Chilled and Hot Water Systems and C-21g Industrial Piping. A full C-21 license covers the work of all its subclassifications.
facts.note: Heating, cooling and circulating-air work can also be licensed under C-1f (see NAC 624.190).

facts.source: Nevada State Contractors Board, Contractor's License Application, https://www.nvcontractorsboard.com/licensing/contractors-license-application/
facts.fact: For a Nevada contractor's license in a trade such as electrical (C-2), plumbing and heating (C-1) or refrigeration and air conditioning (C-21), the trade qualified individual needs at least 4 years of experience in that trade, gained within the past 15 years. The management qualified individual must pass the business and law (CMS) exam, and one person can fill both roles.

facts.source: NAC 341.045, Standards for design (via Cornell LII), https://www.law.cornell.edu/regulations/nevada/NAC-341-045 ; Nevada State Public Works Division, 2024 Adopted Codes, https://publicworks.nv.gov/uploadedFiles/publicworksnvgov/content/Documents/Permitting_Code_Enforcement/2024%20Adopted_Codes.pdf
facts.fact: For the design of Nevada state buildings, NAC 341.045 adopts the 2023 National Electrical Code along with the 2024 IBC, IRC and IEBC. These state rules cover state buildings; cities and counties adopt their own codes for private projects.
facts.note: The State Public Works Division says projects submitted after the grace period ended June 30, 2025 must be designed under the new codes. Local editions vary, so check the city or county.

facts.source: NAC 341.045, Standards for design (via Cornell LII), https://www.law.cornell.edu/regulations/nevada/NAC-341-045
facts.fact: For Nevada state buildings, NAC 341.045 puts the Uniform Plumbing Code in place of the International Plumbing Code. It adopts the 2024 Uniform Plumbing Code and the 2024 Uniform Mechanical Code alongside the 2024 IBC.
facts.note: Applies to state buildings designed under the State Public Works Division. Local jurisdictions adopt their own plumbing and mechanical codes.

facts.source: RSA 155-A:1, IV (state building code definition), https://gc.nh.gov/rsa/html/XII/155-A/155-A-1.htm ; HB 134 (2025), 2025 Laws ch. 135
facts.fact: New Hampshire's state building code (RSA 155-A:1, IV) adopts the 2023 National Electrical Code. HB 134 (2025 Laws chapter 135) moved the state from the 2020 to the 2023 NEC, effective July 1, 2025.
facts.note: When checked in October 2026, the State Fire Marshal's code page (https://firemarshal.dos.nh.gov/laws-rules-regulatory/fire-building-codes) still listed the 2020 NEC. The statute text is current.

facts.source: RSA 155-A:1, IV, https://gc.nh.gov/rsa/html/XII/155-A/155-A-1.htm ; HB 1159 (2026), 2026 Laws ch. 49
facts.fact: New Hampshire uses the International Plumbing Code statewide. HB 1159 (2026 Laws chapter 49) updated the state building code to the 2024 IPC, along with the 2024 IBC, IRC, IEBC and IMC, effective July 1, 2026. Before that, the 2021 editions had applied since July 1, 2024.
facts.note: The energy code stays at the 2018 IECC. The Fire Marshal's page still showed the 2021 editions when checked; check for any concurrency period.

facts.source: RSA 155-A:1, IV, https://gc.nh.gov/rsa/html/XII/155-A/155-A-1.htm
facts.fact: The New Hampshire state building code adopts the 2024 International Mechanical Code, effective July 1, 2026, replacing the 2021 IMC. The energy code part of the state building code remains the 2018 IECC.
facts.note: Fuel gas installations are also regulated through state fire code rules and fuel gas fitter licensing; the NFPA 54/58 editions were not confirmed here.

facts.source: RSA 153:28, I(a) (Mechanical Safety and Licensing Board), https://gc.nh.gov/rsa/html/XII/153/153-mrg.htm
facts.fact: New Hampshire licenses fuel gas workers through the Mechanical Safety and Licensing Board (OPLC). A fuel gas installation technician needs 1,000 hours of field experience within 60 months (up to 500 hours may be heating oil work). A fuel gas service technician needs 2,000 hours within 60 months (up to 750 hours of oil work). A fuel gas piping installer needs 1,000 hours of gas piping experience.
facts.note: Approved education can stand in for field experience. Other classes include hearth system technician, domestic appliance technician and fuel gas trainee.

facts.source: RSA 153:27, XV and 153:28, I(a), https://gc.nh.gov/rsa/html/XII/153/153-mrg.htm
facts.fact: In New Hampshire, a plumbing licensee may employ no more than 2 plumbing apprentices. The Mechanical Safety and Licensing Board sets the education, field experience and testing standards for master, journeyman and apprentice plumber licenses by rule.

facts.source: NJ DCA, Current Construction Codes (N.J.A.C. 5:23-3.16), https://www.nj.gov/dca/codes/codreg/current.shtml
facts.fact: New Jersey's Uniform Construction Code electrical subcode (N.J.A.C. 5:23-3.16) adopts the 2023 National Electrical Code (NFPA 70) with TIAs 1-13. DCA lists the adoption date as August 17, 2026.
facts.note: DCA usually allows a six-month grace period after a new subcode is adopted, during which a complete application may use the prior edition (the 2020 NEC, adopted September 6, 2022). Confirm the current grace period dates with DCA.

facts.source: NJ DCA, Current Construction Codes (N.J.A.C. 5:23-3.15), https://www.nj.gov/dca/codes/codreg/current.shtml
facts.fact: New Jersey uses neither the IPC nor the UPC. Its UCC plumbing subcode (N.J.A.C. 5:23-3.15) adopts the National Standard Plumbing Code, 2024 edition (New Jersey edition), with an adoption date of August 17, 2026.
facts.note: The prior edition was the 2021 NSPC (adopted September 19, 2022). A six-month grace period for the prior edition has been DCA's usual practice.

facts.source: NJ DCA, Current Construction Codes (N.J.A.C. 5:23-3.20 and 3.22), https://www.nj.gov/dca/codes/codreg/current.shtml
facts.fact: Under New Jersey's Uniform Construction Code, the mechanical subcode (N.J.A.C. 5:23-3.20) adopts the 2024 International Mechanical Code, and the fuel gas subcode (N.J.A.C. 5:23-3.22) adopts the 2024 International Fuel Gas Code. Both have an adoption date of August 17, 2026.
facts.note: One- and two-family dwellings use the 2024 IRC (NJ edition) under N.J.A.C. 5:23-3.21.

facts.source: NJ Board of Examiners of Electrical Contractors, FAQ, https://njconsumeraffairs.gov/elec/Pages/FAQ.aspx
facts.fact: The New Jersey electrical contractor exam has three parts: electrical contractor (trade), alarm systems, and business and law. Applicants must show a completed 4-year U.S. Department of Labor approved apprenticeship plus one more year as a journeyman. Electrical contractor licenses and business permits expire every three years on March 31.
facts.note: The FAQ also says a person must register as a qualified journeyman electrician to do the work described in N.J.S.A. 45:5A-18(k) and (l).

facts.source: NJ State Board of Examiners of Master HVACR Contractors, FAQ (N.J.A.C. 13:32A-2.1), https://njconsumeraffairs.gov/hvacr/Pages/FAQ.aspx
facts.fact: To take the New Jersey Master HVACR exam, an applicant needs one of these: a 4-year U.S. DOL approved HVACR apprenticeship plus 1 year as a journeyperson under a licensed Master HVACR Contractor; a bachelor's degree in HVACR plus 1 year; a related bachelor's degree plus 3 years; or a two-year trade school degree plus at least 2 years of approved apprenticeship and 1 year as a journeyperson. Licensees need 5 continuing education credits every two years.

facts.source: 14.10.4 NMAC, 2020 New Mexico Electrical Code, https://www.srca.nm.gov/parts/title14/14.010.0004.pdf
facts.fact: New Mexico's electrical code is 14.10.4 NMAC, the 2020 New Mexico Electrical Code. It adopts the 2020 National Electrical Code with state amendments and took effect March 28, 2023.
facts.note: No newer NEC adoption was found on New Mexico state sites as of October 2026. CID posted drafts for other 2024-cycle codes in 2026, so check for updates.

facts.source: 14.8.2 NMAC, 2021 New Mexico Plumbing Code, https://www.srca.nm.gov/parts/title14/14.008.0002.pdf ; draft 2024 rule, https://www.rld.nm.gov/wp-content/uploads/2026/03/14.8.2-NMAC_DRAFT-RULE.pdf
facts.fact: New Mexico uses the Uniform Plumbing Code. 14.8.2 NMAC, the 2021 New Mexico Plumbing Code, adopts the 2021 UPC with state amendments, and after September 10, 2022 plumbing permits may be issued only under it.
facts.note: In March 2026 CID posted a draft rule that would adopt the 2024 UPC as the 2024 New Mexico Plumbing Code. It was a draft when checked, so confirm whether it has taken effect.

facts.source: 14.9.2 NMAC, 2021 New Mexico Mechanical Code, https://www.srca.nm.gov/parts/title14/14.009.0002.pdf
facts.fact: New Mexico uses the Uniform Mechanical Code. 14.9.2 NMAC, the 2021 New Mexico Mechanical Code, adopts the 2021 UMC with state amendments.
facts.note: A 2024-cycle update may follow the 2024 UPC draft; check the CID site.

facts.source: 14.6.6.11 NMAC, Mechanical classifications, https://www.srca.nm.gov/parts/title14/14.006.0006.pdf
facts.fact: New Mexico's mechanical license classifications are MM-1 plumbing, MM-2 natural gas fitting, MM-3 heating, ventilation and air conditioning (HVAC), MM-4 hydronic heating, cooling and process piping, and MM-98 mechanical, which covers all of MM-1 through MM-4. Each requires four years of experience for the qualifying party.
facts.note: MM-98 also covers the MS-3, MS-6, MS-12 and MS-14 specialty work.

facts.source: 14.6.6.11 NMAC, Mechanical classifications, https://www.srca.nm.gov/parts/title14/14.006.0006.pdf
facts.fact: In New Mexico, an MM-1 plumbing classification requires four years of experience for the qualifying party. The JPG journeyman certificate (journeyman plumber and natural gas fitter) requires two years of experience, and the holder may work under an MM-1, MM-2 or MM-98 licensee.

facts.source: 14.6.6.10 NMAC, Electrical classifications, https://www.srca.nm.gov/parts/title14/14.006.0006.pdf
facts.fact: New Mexico's EE-98 classification covers residential, commercial and industrial electrical wiring at 5,000 volts nominal or less and requires four years of experience. ER-1 (residential) requires two years, EL-1 (over 5,000 volts) requires four years, and the ES electrical specialty classes require two years each.
facts.note: The EE-98J journeyman certificate requires four years and may work under EE-98, ER-1 and the electrical specialty licenses.

facts.source: NYS Department of State, Amended Notice of Adoption, https://dos.ny.gov/notice-adoption ; NYSED Facilities Planning notice, https://www.nysed.gov/facilities-planning/news/2025-nys-uniform-code-and-state-energy-code-will-take-effect-december-31
facts.fact: The 2025 New York State Uniform Code, including the 2025 Plumbing Code of New York State, took effect December 31, 2025. The 2025 NYS code books are based on the 2024 ICC model codes with New York changes. From October 1 to December 30, 2025, applicants could use either the 2020 or the 2025 Uniform Code.
facts.note: Basis on 2024 ICC books per DOS Code Outreach bulletin 2026-1 (https://dos.ny.gov/2026-01-nycrr-changes-2025-codes). New York City has its own construction codes.
keywords: Plumbing Code of New York State

facts.source: NYS Department of State, Amended Notice of Adoption, https://dos.ny.gov/notice-adoption
facts.fact: New York's 2025 Uniform Code, effective December 31, 2025, includes the 2025 Mechanical Code of New York State and the 2025 Fuel Gas Code of New York State. Both are based on the 2024 ICC model codes (IMC and IFGC) with New York changes.
facts.note: The energy code had no transition period. New York City uses its own mechanical and fuel gas codes.
keywords: Fuel Gas Code of New York State

facts.source: NYC Electrical Code section 28-1101.1, NYC Department of Buildings, https://www.nyc.gov/assets/buildings/codes-pdf/2025electrical_code.pdf
facts.fact: New York City has its own electrical code. Section 28-1101.1 of the NYC Electrical Code adopts the 2020 edition of NFPA 70 (the National Electrical Code) with New York City amendments.
facts.note: This applies in NYC only. Outside the city, electrical work follows the state Uniform Code and local rules.

facts.source: NYS Department of State, Code Outreach bulletin 2026-1, https://dos.ny.gov/2026-01-nycrr-changes-2025-codes
facts.fact: Outside New York City, electrical installations fall under the NYS Uniform Code, which points to NFPA 70. The 2025 Uniform Code (effective December 31, 2025) is based on the 2024 ICC codes, which reference the 2023 NEC, so the 2023 NEC is likely the edition now in force statewide.
facts.note: No official NYS page that names the NEC edition in the 2025 Uniform Code was found. The 2023 NEC is inferred from the 2024 ICC base codes. New York has no statewide electrician license (see STAT-280).

facts.source: NYC Department of Buildings, Obtain a Master & Special Electrician License, https://www.nyc.gov/site/buildings/industry/obtain-a-master-and-special-electrician-license.page
facts.fact: A New York City master electrician applicant must be at least 18 and have at least 7 years of experience within the 10 years before applying, under the direct and continuing supervision of a licensed master or special electrician, with at least 2 years in NYC. Candidates must pass a multiple-choice written exam on NYC electrical codes (70% to pass) and then a practical exam within 24 months.
facts.note: Other routes: a bachelor's degree in electrical engineering plus 3 years within 5, or a NYS DOL registered apprenticeship plus 5 years within 10 (2 years in NYC still required for the degree route).

facts.source: NYC Department of Buildings, Obtain a Master Plumber License, https://www.nyc.gov/site/buildings/industry/obtain-a-master-plumber-license.page
facts.fact: A New York City master plumber applicant needs 7 years of experience within the 10 years before applying, under a licensed master plumber, including at least 2 years as a registered journeyman plumber. The written exam is multiple-choice on NYC construction codes, with no reference materials allowed and a 70% passing score. The practical exam must be passed within 24 months of the written exam notice.
facts.note: Other routes include a mechanical engineering degree plus 5 years within 7 (2 in NYC) or a NYS-licensed architect or engineer with 3 years within 5 (1 in NYC).

facts.source: NC Office of State Fire Marshal, State Electrical Code and Interpretations, https://ncosfm.gov/codes/state-electrical-division/state-electrical-code-and-interpretations
facts.fact: North Carolina's current electrical code is the 2020 NEC with state amendments, in effect since November 1, 2021. The 2023 NEC with NC amendments was set for January 1, 2025, but Session Law 2025-2 (House Bill 47) delayed it with no set date.
facts.note: Under S.L. 2025-2, the 2024 code package, including the 2023 NC Electrical Code, takes effect 12 months after the State Fire Marshal certifies certain conditions. Check OSFM for the current status.

facts.source: NC OSFM press release, North Carolina Delays Implementation of 2024 State Building Code (Apr. 7, 2025), https://ncosfm.gov/news/press-releases/2025/04/07/north-carolina-delays-implementation-2024-state-building-code
facts.fact: The 2018 North Carolina State Building Code, including the 2018 NC Plumbing Code, remains in effect. Session Law 2025-2 moved the 2024 NC State Building Code to 12 months after the State Fire Marshal certifies the code is published and the Residential Code Council is fully formed. An owner may ask to use the 2024 code as an alternative method.
facts.note: The State Fire Marshal's letter of March 31, 2025 calls the date 'to be determined'. Check OSFM for whether the certification has been made.

facts.source: NC OSFM, Effective Date of the 2024 NC State Building Code memo, https://ncosfm.gov/2024-1212-effective-date-2024-north-carolina-state-building-code/open ; OSFM press release Apr. 7, 2025
facts.fact: North Carolina's 2018 Mechanical Code and 2018 Fuel Gas Code are still in force because the 2024 NC State Building Code was delayed (first by S.L. 2024-57 to July 1, 2025, then by S.L. 2025-2 to 12 months after State Fire Marshal certification). A project that chooses the 2024 code early must use it for the whole project scope.
facts.note: Check OSFM for the certification date that starts the 12-month clock.

facts.source: 21 NCAC 18B .0201, Requirements for all examination applicants (via Cornell LII), https://law.cornell.edu/regulations/north-carolina/21-N-C-Admin-Code-18B-0201
facts.fact: To take the North Carolina electrical contractor exam, a Limited applicant needs 3,000 hours of experience (at least 2,000 primary), an Intermediate applicant needs 5,750 hours (at least 5,000 primary), and an Unlimited applicant needs 9,000 hours (at least 8,000 primary). Unlimited applicants must also submit written statements from two people who can vouch for their ability to supervise electrical work.
facts.note: Primary and secondary experience are defined in 21 NCAC 18B .0202.

facts.source: N.C. Gen. Stat. 87-21, https://www.ncleg.gov/EnactedLegislation/Statutes/HTML/BySection/Chapter_87/GS_87-21.html
facts.fact: Under N.C. Gen. Stat. 87-21, the State Board of Examiners of Plumbing, Heating and Fire Sprinkler Contractors may require no more than two years of experience to take its exam, and up to half of that may come from academic or technical courses. A plumbing or heating licensee who has kept a license in good standing for at least 10 years is credited with the experience for Class II qualifications.
facts.note: Applicants may be required to be at least 18.

facts.source: N.C. Gen. Stat. 87-21, https://www.ncleg.gov/EnactedLegislation/Statutes/HTML/BySection/Chapter_87/GS_87-21.html
facts.fact: North Carolina's plumbing, heating and fire sprinkler board issues a separate fuel piping license for people who do not hold the needed Class I or Class II plumbing or heating license. Heating licenses are split into three groups, and group three covers systems of 15 tons or less (see STAT-294).

facts.source: N.D. Admin. Code 24.1-02-01-02 and 24.1-02-01-03, https://www.ndlegis.gov/information/acdata/pdf/24.1-02-01.pdf
facts.fact: North Dakota's State Electrical Board wiring standards adopt the 2026 edition of NFPA 70, the National Electrical Code, effective July 1, 2026. North Dakota had been on the 2023 NEC since July 1, 2024.
facts.note: The rule history shows amendments effective July 1, 2024 and July 1, 2026. The July 1, 2024 move to the 2023 NEC is reported by Interstate IBC (https://interstateibc.org/nd-adopts-2023-nec/). Exam references may lag; check the PSI bulletin.

facts.source: N.D. Admin. Code 62-03.1-01-01, https://www.ndlegis.gov/information/acdata/pdf/62-03.1-01.pdf
facts.fact: The North Dakota State Plumbing Board adopts the 2018 Uniform Plumbing Code (IAPMO) as the state plumbing code, known as the 2018 North Dakota Plumbing Code. The rule took effect April 1, 2020.
facts.note: This was the current posted rule as of October 2026. A newer UPC edition may be adopted later.

facts.source: ND Department of Commerce, Building Codes, https://www.commerce.nd.gov/community-services/building-codes
facts.fact: The North Dakota State Building Code, which includes the 2024 International Mechanical Code and 2024 International Fuel Gas Code along with the 2024 IBC and IRC, took effect January 1, 2026. Local governments do not have to enforce building codes, but any jurisdiction that chooses to must use the State Building Code, with local amendments allowed.
facts.note: Fully chartered home rule cities may adopt something else. North Dakota has no statewide HVAC license (not confirmed on an official page).

facts.source: N.D. Admin. Code 62-02-01-01, https://www.ndlegis.gov/information/acdata/pdf/62-02-01.pdf
facts.fact: To take the North Dakota journeyman plumber exam, an applicant needs four years of experience as an apprentice plumber under a licensed master plumber. The master plumber exam requires an applicant to be at least 21 with two years (3,400 hours) as a licensed journeyman plumber in North Dakota or another licensing state.
facts.note: Someone who worked where no state license is required may instead show five years in the trade (1,900 hours a year, 9,500 hours total) with four affidavits and pass a screening test first.

facts.source: Union County (OH) Building Regulation, Current Ohio Code References (1/28/2026), https://www.unioncountyohio.gov/media/Officials/Engineer/building-regulation/BuildingInUnionCo_UsefulInfo/Current%20Ohio%20Code%20References.pdf ; OAC 4101:1-27-01 (eff. 3/1/2024)
facts.fact: Ohio enforces the 2023 National Electrical Code for commercial buildings under the Ohio Building Code since March 1, 2024, and for one-, two- and three-family homes under the Residential Code of Ohio since April 15, 2024. Before that, Ohio used the 2017 NEC.
facts.note: Confirmed on a county building department page and consistent with the OCILB electrical exam, which uses the 2023 NEC (STAT-309). A Board of Building Standards page naming the edition was not reached.

facts.source: ICC news release, Ohio Strengthens Building Safety and Resilience by Adopting International Plumbing, Building and Mechanical Codes, https://www.iccsafe.org/about/periodicals-and-newsroom/ohio-strengthens-building-safety-and-resilience-by-adopting-international-plumbing-building-and-mechanical-codes ; Ohio BBS 2024 OPC Summary of Changes
facts.fact: The 2024 Ohio Plumbing Code is based on the 2021 International Plumbing Code with Ohio changes and took effect March 1, 2024. One Ohio change adds a small-business exception to the toilet room requirements in section 403.2.
facts.note: The edition and date are from the ICC release. The Ohio Board of Building Standards summary (https://dam.assets.ohio.gov/image/upload/com.ohio.gov/documents/2024%20OPC%20Summary%20of%20Changes%20-%20BBS%20letterhead.pdf) confirms adoption of the IPC by reference and lists the changes.

facts.source: ICC news release (Ohio adopts 2021 I-Codes, effective March 1, 2024); Union County (OH) Current Ohio Code References, https://www.unioncountyohio.gov/media/Officials/Engineer/building-regulation/BuildingInUnionCo_UsefulInfo/Current%20Ohio%20Code%20References.pdf
facts.fact: Ohio's commercial mechanical code is the 2024 Ohio Mechanical Code, based on the 2021 International Mechanical Code and effective March 1, 2024. Commercial fuel gas work follows the 2021 International Fuel Gas Code.
facts.note: This replaced the 2017 OMC and the 2015 IFGC. Homes follow the Residential Code of Ohio.

facts.source: Ohio Rev. Code 4740.06(B), https://codes.ohio.gov/ohio-revised-code/section-4740.06
facts.fact: To take an Ohio Construction Industry Licensing Board exam (electrical, plumbing, HVAC, refrigeration or hydronics), an applicant must be at least 18 and have worked at least five years as a tradesperson in that trade right before applying, or have other experience the specialty section accepts. An Ohio-registered engineer may instead qualify with three years of construction business experience in that trade.
facts.note: Licensees must also carry contractor's liability insurance in an amount set by the specialty section.

facts.source: Oklahoma Construction Industries Board news, 2023 NEC Code (Aug. 20, 2024), https://oklahoma.gov/cib/news/2023-nec-code.html
facts.fact: The Oklahoma Uniform Building Code Commission adopted the 2023 National Electrical Code, effective September 14, 2024. CIB electrical exam questions stayed on the 2020 NEC through December 13, 2024 and switched to the 2023 NEC on December 14, 2024.

facts.source: OUBCC, 2024 IPC rules (OAC 748:20-16), https://oklahoma.gov/content/dam/ok/en/oubcc/documents/2024-pending-rules/2024%20IPC%20Pending%20Rules.pdf ; CIB news, 2026 Updated Building Code, https://oklahoma.gov/cib/news/2026-updated-building-code.html
facts.fact: Oklahoma's statewide plumbing code is the International Plumbing Code. The OUBCC adopted the 2024 IPC (OAC 748:20-16), effective September 14, 2026, replacing the 2018 IPC. The 2021 IPC was never adopted in Oklahoma.

facts.source: Oklahoma Construction Industries Board news, 2026 Updated Building Code (Aug. 31, 2026), https://oklahoma.gov/cib/news/2026-updated-building-code.html
facts.fact: Oklahoma adopted the 2024 International Mechanical Code and 2024 International Fuel Gas Code (with the 2024 IBC, IRC and IPC), effective September 14, 2026. CIB mechanical exams such as HVACR, refrigeration, sheet metal, natural gas and process piping moved to the new codes that day, with a 90-day transition through December 14, 2026 when either code may be used.
facts.note: The Plumbing Contractor and the Plumbing Journeyman and Gas exams change on October 8, 2026, with a transition through January 8, 2027.

facts.source: Oklahoma CIB Plumbing License Application (rev. 9-2023), https://aem-prod.oklahoma.gov/content/dam/ok/en/cib/documents/your-industry/plumbing-industry/plumbing_application-9-2023.pdf
facts.fact: Oklahoma plumbers are licensed statewide by the Construction Industries Board. A plumbing journeyman needs three years of plumbing experience while employed by a licensed plumbing contractor, and a plumbing contractor needs the journeyman requirements plus one more year. CIB counts one year of full-time work as about 2,000 hours.
facts.note: A residential plumbing contractor needs the residential journeyman requirements plus one year. Requirements are from the 2023 application form; check CIB for later rule changes.

facts.source: Oklahoma Construction Industries Board, Mechanical Journeyman, https://oklahoma.gov/cib/your-industry/mechanical/mechanical-journeyman.html
facts.fact: Oklahoma's CIB licenses mechanical journeymen in categories such as HVAC Limited (cooling up to 25 tons and heating up to 500,000 Btu/h per appliance), HVAC Unlimited, Limited Residential, Refrigeration, Natural Gas Piping, Process Piping and Sheet Metal. The basic route is age 18 plus three years of verifiable experience with a licensed mechanical contractor, where one year equals 2,000 hours. Approved school programs can replace part of the experience.
facts.note: Examples: a 1,000-hour program plus 1 year, or a 500-hour program plus 2 years. Limited Residential covers new one- and two-family homes with systems up to 5 tons cooling and 150,000 Btu/h heating, with no fuel gas piping.

facts.source: Oregon Building Codes Division, Electrical (Oregon Electrical Specialty Code), https://oregon.gov/bcd/codes-stand/Pages/electrical.aspx
facts.fact: Oregon's electrical code is the Oregon Electrical Specialty Code (OESC). The 2026 OESC is based on the 2026 National Electrical Code and took effect October 1, 2026.
facts.note: The BCD page did not mention a phase-in period. The prior edition was the 2023 OESC.

facts.source: Oregon Building Codes Division, Plumbing (Oregon Plumbing Specialty Code), https://www.oregon.gov/bcd/codes-stand/Pages/plumbing.aspx
facts.fact: Oregon uses the Uniform Plumbing Code as the base for its Oregon Plumbing Specialty Code (OPSC). The 2026 OPSC is based on the 2024 UPC and took effect October 1, 2026. It replaced the 2023 OPSC, which was based on the 2021 UPC and took effect October 1, 2023.
facts.note: The BCD page did not describe a phase-in period for the 2026 OPSC.

facts.source: Oregon Building Codes Division, Mechanical (Oregon Mechanical Specialty Code), https://www.oregon.gov/bcd/codes-stand/Pages/mechanical.aspx
facts.fact: The 2025 Oregon Mechanical Specialty Code (OMSC) is based on the 2024 International Mechanical Code and International Fuel Gas Code. It took effect October 1, 2025 with a six-month phase-in, when either the 2022 or 2025 OMSC could be used, and became mandatory April 1, 2026.

facts.source: Oregon BCD, Electrical License Application information packet (Form 440-2570i), https://www.oregon.gov/bcd/Formslibrary/2570i.pdf
facts.fact: An Oregon General Journeyman Electrician (J) license requires an approved Oregon apprenticeship, or 576 hours of classroom training plus 8,000 hours of out-of-state experience (at least 1,000 each in residential, commercial and industrial work), or 16,000 hours of out-of-state experience. A General Supervising Electrician (S) needs a journeyman license (or its qualifications) plus another 8,000 hours of journeyman experience. A Limited Residential Electrician (LR) needs an apprenticeship, 288 classroom hours plus 4,000 residential hours, or 8,000 residential hours.
facts.note: Oregon's '300 percent rule' applies to how out-of-state experience is counted (see the packet).

facts.source: Oregon BCD, Plumbing License Application (Form 440-2571), https://www.oregon.gov/bcd/Formslibrary/2571.pdf
facts.fact: To qualify for the Oregon journeyman plumber (JP) exam, an applicant can show at least 576 hours of plumbing classroom training plus 3,850 hours of commercial and 3,850 hours of residential on-the-job experience as an apprentice or journeyman. Another route is 7,700 hours each of commercial and residential work done while holding a license with a similar scope. No more than 2,000 hours of experience count per year.
facts.note: A high school diploma, GED or equivalent is also required.

facts.source: City of Philadelphia L&I Code Bulletin B-2501, Implementation of 2021 International Codes, https://www.phila.gov/media/20251021080549/B-2501-Implementation-of-2021-International-Codes.pdf ; City of York, 2021 UCC Code Update, https://www.yorkcity.org/2021ucc
facts.fact: Pennsylvania's statewide Uniform Construction Code (UCC) moved to the 2021 International Plumbing Code on January 1, 2026, replacing the 2018 editions. Applications complete and submitted before that date could continue under the 2018 UCC.
facts.note: Confirmed by two municipal code offices citing PA Department of Labor & Industry rulemaking (Pa. Bulletin Doc. No. 25-1602). The DLI and Pa. Code pages could not be fetched. Philadelphia and Allegheny County have their own plumbing rules.

facts.source: City of Philadelphia L&I Code Bulletin B-2501, https://www.phila.gov/media/20251021080549/B-2501-Implementation-of-2021-International-Codes.pdf ; City of York, 2021 UCC Code Update, https://www.yorkcity.org/2021ucc
facts.fact: Since January 1, 2026, Pennsylvania's Uniform Construction Code uses the 2021 International Mechanical Code and 2021 International Fuel Gas Code, along with the 2021 IBC and IRC.
facts.note: Confirmed by two municipal code offices citing DLI's adoption under the PA Construction Code Act (Act 45 of 1999).

facts.source: City of Philadelphia L&I Code Bulletin B-2501, https://www.phila.gov/media/20251021080549/B-2501-Implementation-of-2021-International-Codes.pdf ; City of York, 2021 UCC Code Update, https://www.yorkcity.org/2021ucc
facts.fact: Under Pennsylvania's 2021 Uniform Construction Code (effective January 1, 2026), the referenced electrical standard is the 2020 NFPA 70 (National Electrical Code), not the 2023 edition.
facts.note: Confirmed by Philadelphia L&I and the City of York. Pennsylvania has no statewide electrician license (see STAT-342).

facts.source: City of Philadelphia, Get an electrical contractor license, https://www.phila.gov/services/permits-violations-licenses/get-a-license/trade-licenses/get-an-electrical-contractor-license/
facts.fact: Pennsylvania leaves electrician licensing to local governments. In Philadelphia, an electrical contractor license requires at least four years of electrical work for a licensed company (two years of electrical school count as one year, up to two years) and a passing score on the Philadelphia Electrical Contractor Examination given by the ICC. Licensees need at least $500,000 per occurrence of general liability insurance.
facts.note: Auto liability of $300,000 and workers' compensation are also required.

facts.source: Allegheny County Health Department, Plumbers Exam Application, https://www.alleghenycounty.us/files/assets/county/v/2/government/health/documents/plumbers-exam-application.pdf
facts.fact: In Allegheny County (Pittsburgh area), plumbers are licensed by the county Health Department. A journeyman plumber needs four full years as a registered apprentice plus 576 hours of related technical training, and a master plumber needs two full years as a licensed journeyman. The exams are based on Article XV, the county plumbing code, which uses the 2009 International Plumbing Code as amended.
facts.note: The edition is from the county exam application; check ACHD for any newer Article XV edition.

facts.source: RISBC-5 Rhode Island Electrical Code (510-RICR-00-00-5), section 5.2(A), https://rules.sos.ri.gov/Regulations/Part/510-00-00-5
facts.fact: Rhode Island's state electrical code, RISBC-5, adopts the 2023 edition of the National Electrical Code. The current version of the rule took effect December 1, 2025.

facts.source: RISBC-3 Rhode Island Plumbing Code (510-RICR-00-00-3), section 3.2, https://rules.sos.ri.gov/Regulations/Part/510-00-00-3
facts.fact: Rhode Island's state plumbing code, RISBC-3, adopts the 2021 International Plumbing Code. The current version of the rule took effect December 1, 2025.

facts.source: RISBC-4 Rhode Island Mechanical Code (510-RICR-00-00-4), https://rules.sos.ri.gov/Regulations/Part/510-00-00-4
facts.fact: Rhode Island's mechanical code, RISBC-4, adopts the 2021 International Mechanical Code (current version effective December 1, 2025). Wherever the IMC refers to the International Fuel Gas Code, Rhode Island uses its own Rhode Island Fuel Gas Code instead.

facts.source: RI Department of Labor and Training, Electricians License Application, https://dlt.ri.gov/sites/g/files/xkgbur571/files/2024-05/applicationelectricians_0_0.pdf
facts.fact: Rhode Island's Class B journeyperson electrician exam requires at least four years of experience in the trade and 576 hours of related instruction approved by the Department of Labor and Training. The Class A electrical contractor exam requires six years of experience and a Rhode Island journeyperson license held for at least two years.
facts.note: Indentured apprentices submit a Certificate of Completion of Apprenticeship.

facts.source: R.I. Gen. Laws 5-20-17, https://webserver.rilegislature.gov/Statutes/TITLE5/5-20/5-20-17.htm
facts.fact: A Rhode Island journeyperson plumber applicant must generally have been a registered apprentice plumber for at least four years, with 8,000 hours of on-the-job training in Rhode Island within five years, plus 576 hours of related instruction. Other routes include two academic years of plumbing or sanitary engineering study, an associate degree plus two years as a registered apprentice, or an equivalent out-of-state journeyperson license.
facts.note: The apprentice and the master plumber record the apprenticeship hours together.

facts.source: R.I. Gen. Laws 28-27-5, https://webserver.rilegislature.gov/Statutes/TITLE28/28-27/28-27-5.htm
facts.fact: In Rhode Island, working as a master in pipefitting, refrigeration/air conditioning, air distribution or fire sprinkler work requires a license from the Department of Labor and Training. A master license holder may do the sheet metal work on a job without a separate license only when the AC air handling equipment is 10 tons or less or the heating equipment is 250,000 BTU or less. Larger jobs must use a licensed sheet metal contractor.

facts.source: SC LLR Building Codes Council, Building Codes in Effect for South Carolina, https://www.llr.sc.gov/BCC/PDFfiles/Building%20Codes%20in%20Effect%20for%20South%20Carolina.pdf ; Building Code Adoption, https://llr.sc.gov/bcc/BCAdoption.aspx
facts.fact: South Carolina's mandatory statewide electrical code is the 2020 National Electrical Code with SC modifications. The Building Codes Council adopted it October 6, 2021, and local jurisdictions had to put it in place by January 1, 2023.
facts.note: The Council is adopting the 2024 code cycle: SC changes to it were published in the State Register on May 22, 2026, but no effective date was posted when checked (October 2026). Check whether the 2023 NEC is part of that cycle.

facts.source: SC LLR Building Codes Council, SC Code Adoption Notice, https://www.llr.sc.gov/bcc/pdffiles/SC-Code-Adoption-Notice.pdf
facts.fact: South Carolina uses the International Plumbing Code statewide. The 2021 IPC with SC modifications has been in effect since January 1, 2023, when local jurisdictions had to begin using the 2021 code cycle.
facts.note: The 2024 code cycle was in progress in 2026 with no effective date posted yet.

facts.source: SC LLR Building Codes Council, Building Codes in Effect for South Carolina, https://www.llr.sc.gov/BCC/PDFfiles/Building%20Codes%20in%20Effect%20for%20South%20Carolina.pdf
facts.fact: South Carolina's statewide mechanical and fuel gas codes are the 2021 International Mechanical Code and 2021 International Fuel Gas Code, both with SC modifications and in effect since January 1, 2023.
facts.note: The previous editions (2018 IMC/IFGC) took effect January 1, 2020.

facts.source: SC LLR Residential Builders Commission, Residential HVAC Installer and Repairer License, https://www.llr.sc.gov/res/reshvac.aspx
facts.fact: In South Carolina, residential HVAC work over $500 requires a Residential HVAC license from the Residential Builders Commission, with verified work experience and the SC Residential HVAC exam. Commercial HVAC work over $10,000 needs a mechanical contractor license from the Contractor's Licensing Board instead.
facts.note: An exam waiver skips only the technical part. The experience requirement and the Business Management and Law exam still apply.

facts.source: SC LLR Residential Builders Commission, Licensure, https://llr.sc.gov/res/licensure.aspx
facts.fact: South Carolina's Residential Builders Commission issues residential specialty licenses for electrical (RBE), HVAC (RBH) and plumbing (RBP) work. Licensure by exam requires passing the PSI exam and one year of verifiable experience under a licensed person in that trade. North Carolina and Mississippi licensees may get a trade exam waiver but must still pass the SC Business Management and Law exam.
facts.note: The NASCLA electrical exam is also accepted. A separate Residential Specialty Contractor Registration (RBS) requires one year of residential experience in the past five years per trade.

questions.q: Which edition of the National Electrical Code did Nebraska's State Electrical Division adopt effective August 1, 2024?
questions.why: Nebraska adopted the 2023 NEC (NFPA 70) starting August 1, 2024, and PSI exams moved to the 2023 code that day.

questions.q: How much verifiable experience does Nebraska require for a journeyman electrician license?
questions.why: Nebraska requires at least four years (8,000 hours) of verifiable electrical experience for the journeyman license.

questions.q: Which plumbing code is part of Nebraska's state building code under Neb. Rev. Stat. 71-6403?
questions.why: The Nebraska state building code adopts the 2018 Uniform Plumbing Code along with the 2018 IBC, IRC and IEBC.

questions.q: In Nevada, which State Contractors Board classification covers refrigeration and air-conditioning contracting?
questions.why: Classification C-21 is refrigeration and air-conditioning, with subclassifications C-21a through C-21g.

questions.q: How much trade experience does Nevada require of a contractor license's trade qualified individual?
questions.why: The NSCB requires at least 4 years of experience in the trade, gained within the past 15 years.

questions.q: Since July 1, 2025, which NEC edition is part of the New Hampshire state building code?
questions.why: HB 134 (2025 Laws ch. 135) changed the state building code from the 2020 to the 2023 NEC effective July 1, 2025.

questions.q: Which plumbing code does New Jersey adopt in its Uniform Construction Code plumbing subcode?
c: A New Jersey plumbing code with no model code base
questions.why: New Jersey's plumbing subcode adopts the National Standard Plumbing Code (2024, NJ edition), not the IPC or UPC.

questions.q: The New Jersey electrical contractor exam has three parts. Which list is correct?
c: Trade, alarm systems, and business and law
Business and law, OSHA, and load calculations
Trade, fire sprinklers, and energy code
questions.why: The NJ Board says the exam covers electrical contractor (trade), alarm systems, and business and law.

questions.q: Which model plumbing code does New Mexico adopt for its state plumbing code (14.8.2 NMAC)?
questions.why: The 2021 New Mexico Plumbing Code adopts the 2021 Uniform Plumbing Code with state amendments.

questions.q: In New Mexico, which mechanical classification covers heating, ventilation and air conditioning (HVAC)?
questions.why: MM-3 is HVAC. MM-1 is plumbing, MM-2 is natural gas fitting, and MM-4 is hydronic heating, cooling and process piping.

questions.q: A New York City master electrician applicant generally needs how much experience under a licensed master or special electrician?
questions.ref: NYC DOB Master Electrician License page
questions.why: NYC DOB requires at least 7 years of experience within the 10 years before applying, with at least 2 years in NYC.

questions.q: When did the 2025 New York State Uniform Code, including the 2025 Plumbing Code of NYS, take effect?
questions.why: The 2025 Uniform Code took effect December 31, 2025, after a transition period from October 1 to December 30, 2025.

questions.q: As of 2026, which NEC edition is North Carolina's electrical code based on?
questions.ref: NC OSFM State Electrical Code page
questions.why: North Carolina has used the 2020 NEC with state amendments since November 1, 2021. The 2023 NEC was delayed indefinitely by S.L. 2025-2.

questions.q: How many hours of experience does an Unlimited electrical contractor exam applicant need in North Carolina?
questions.why: Unlimited applicants need 9,000 hours (at least 8,000 primary). Limited needs 3,000, and Intermediate needs 5,750.

questions.q: Effective July 1, 2026, which NEC edition do North Dakota's State Electrical Board wiring standards adopt?
questions.why: The ND wiring standards now name the NFPA 70 2026 edition, effective July 1, 2026. The state was on the 2023 NEC from July 1, 2024.

questions.q: Which code is the North Dakota state plumbing code based on?
questions.why: The State Plumbing Board adopts the 2018 UPC as the 2018 North Dakota Plumbing Code.

questions.q: The 2024 Ohio Plumbing Code, effective March 1, 2024, is based on which model code?
questions.why: Ohio adopted the 2021 IPC (with Ohio changes) as the 2024 Ohio Plumbing Code, effective March 1, 2024.

questions.q: Under Ohio Rev. Code 4740.06, how many years as a tradesperson must an OCILB exam applicant normally have right before applying?
questions.why: Ohio requires at least five years as a tradesperson in that trade immediately before applying, or three years for an Ohio-registered engineer.

questions.q: Effective September 14, 2026, which plumbing code edition is Oklahoma's statewide minimum?
questions.why: The OUBCC adopted the 2024 IPC effective September 14, 2026, replacing the 2018 IPC. Oklahoma never adopted the 2021 IPC.

questions.q: How much plumbing experience does Oklahoma's CIB require for a plumbing journeyman license?
questions.why: A plumbing journeyman needs three years of experience while employed by a licensed plumbing contractor. A contractor needs one more year.

questions.q: Under Oklahoma's CIB rules, the HVAC Limited mechanical journeyman category covers cooling equipment up to how many tons?
questions.why: HVAC Limited covers cooling up to 25 tons and heating up to 500,000 Btu/h per appliance. HVAC Unlimited has no capacity cap.

questions.q: Which model code is the 2026 Oregon Plumbing Specialty Code based on?
questions.why: The 2026 OPSC, effective October 1, 2026, is based on the 2024 UPC. The 2023 OPSC was based on the 2021 UPC.

questions.q: Which NEC edition is the 2026 Oregon Electrical Specialty Code based on?
questions.why: The 2026 OESC is based on the 2026 NEC and took effect October 1, 2026.

questions.q: An Oregon General Supervising Electrician (S) applicant must hold a journeyman license (or its qualifications) plus how many more hours of journeyman experience?
questions.why: The S license requires verification of an additional 8,000 hours of on-the-job journeyman experience.

questions.q: Since January 1, 2026, which plumbing code does Pennsylvania's statewide Uniform Construction Code use?
c: Pennsylvania has no statewide plumbing code
questions.ref: Phila. L&I Bulletin B-2501; City of York
questions.why: Pennsylvania's UCC moved from the 2018 to the 2021 International Codes, including the 2021 IPC, on January 1, 2026.

questions.q: Which NEC edition is referenced under Pennsylvania's 2021 Uniform Construction Code (effective January 1, 2026)?
questions.ref: Phila. L&I Bulletin B-2501; City of York
questions.why: Both Philadelphia L&I and the City of York list the 2020 NFPA 70 as the electrical standard under the 2021 UCC.

questions.q: Which plumbing code does Rhode Island adopt as RISBC-3?
questions.why: RISBC-3 adopts the 2021 IPC; the current version of the rule took effect December 1, 2025.

questions.q: To take Rhode Island's Class A electrical contractor exam, how long must the applicant have held a Rhode Island journeyperson license?
questions.why: The journeyperson license must be valid at least two years before applying, with six years of total trade experience.

questions.q: In Rhode Island, a mechanical master license holder may do the sheet metal work without a separate license when the AC air handling equipment is no more than:
questions.why: The exception covers AC air handling equipment of 10 tons or less or heating equipment of 250,000 BTU or less.

questions.q: Which NEC edition has been mandatory statewide in South Carolina since January 1, 2023?
questions.why: The SC Building Codes Council adopted the 2020 NEC (with SC changes) on October 6, 2021, effective January 1, 2023.

questions.q: In South Carolina, residential HVAC work over what amount requires a Residential HVAC license?
questions.ref: SC LLR Residential HVAC License page
questions.why: Residential HVAC work over $500 needs the license. Commercial HVAC work over $10,000 falls under the Contractor's Licensing Board.
